name: Melatonin
short: Trial adverse events were few and mostly mild (daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness); long-term data are limited. Drugs acting on CYP1A2 may slow its breakdown.
text: A systematic review of 37 placebo-controlled trials in sleep disorders found few, generally mild to moderate adverse events; the most frequent were daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness and hypothermia, with no life-threatening events, though long-term evidence was scarce. A meta-analysis of higher-dose trials (10 mg or more), based on only four trials at low risk of bias, found no detectable increase in serious adverse events, but an increase in adverse events such as drowsiness, headache and dizziness; the authors describe the evidence as limited. Melatonin is broken down in the liver by CYP1A2, and a review notes that drugs interacting with CYP1A2 are likely to slow its metabolism.

quotes: The most frequently reported AEs were daytime sleepiness (1.66%), headache (0.74%), other sleep-related AEs (0.74%), dizziness (0.74%) and hypothermia (0.62%).
Few, generally mild to moderate, AEs were associated with exogenous melatonin. No AEs that were life threatening or of major clinical significance were identified.
The scarcity of evidence from long-term RCTs, however, limits the conclusions regarding the safety of continuous melatonin therapy over extended periods.
citations.label: Besag et al., 2019, CNS Drugs
citations.title: Adverse Events Associated with Melatonin for the Treatment of Primary or Secondary Sleep Disorders: A Systematic Review.

quotes: Randomised controlled trials investigating high-dose melatonin (≥10 mg) in human adults over 30 years of age were included.
Overall, only four studies met the pre-specified low risk of bias criteria for meta-analysis.
Based on this limited evidence, melatonin appears to have a good safety profile.
melatonin did not cause a detectable increase in SAEs
but did appear to increase the risk of AEs such as drowsiness, headache and dizziness

quotes: Melatonin is rapidly absorbed and undergoes first pass hepatic metabolism by cytochrome CYP1A2
Drugs interacting with CYP1A2 are likely to slow-down melatonin metabolism.
